extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students learning category theory and algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and worked examples about functors, natural transformations, Yoneda lemma, limits (equalizers), abelian categories, and the basics of singular homology (chains, boundary, cycles, homology groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural transformation (via A × 2 → B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural transformation α : F ⇒ G is just a functor α : A × 2 → B satisfying α(−,0) = F and α(−,1) = G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently one may think of α as the family of components α(A) with the usual naturality conditions; the text leaves the proof of equivalence as an exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of natural transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Two natural transformations α : F ⇒ G and β : G ⇒ H can be composed to obtain β ◦ α : F ⇒ H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition is done componentwise (diagrammatic depiction in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural transformation α : F ⇒ G is a natural isomorphism if each component α_A is an isomorphism (so one can choose inverses β_A giving an inverse natural transformation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation: F ≅ G indicates F and G are naturally isomorphic; this is the formal meaning of 'canonical' isomorphism (example: (V^∨)^∨ ≅ V naturally in V ∈ FDVect_k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functor category [A,B]
rubrics_metrics.description: The functor category [A,B] has as objects covariant functors F : A → B and as morphisms natural transformations α : F ⇒ G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question posed: When are two objects in the functor category isomorphic? — i.e., when are two functors naturally isomorphic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yoneda lemma (characterization of maps to representables)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A ∈ A and a contravariant functor X : A^op → Set, the map Natural(HA, X) → X(A) given by α ↦ α_A(id_A) is a bijection (and this bijection is natural in both arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies natural transformations into a representable functor HA with elements of X(A); see text for intuitive explanation and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable presheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: A presheaf X (a contravariant functor A^op → Set) is called representable if X ≅ H_A for some object A ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: 'what presheaves are already built into the category A?'; representability can be tested via the Yoneda lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yoneda embedding is fully faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment H_• : A → [A^op, Set] gives a functor which is fully faithful, i.e. it embeds A into the functor category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: H_X ≅ H_Y ⇔ X ≅ Y; the embedding is analogous to Cayley's theorem for groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of a covariant functor (existence condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A covariant functor X : A → Set is represented by an object A ∈ A and an element u ∈ X(A) when for all A' ∈ A and x ∈ X(A') there exists a unique f : A → A' with (X f)(u) = x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition is the concrete form of a represention H_A ≅ X (text gives the condition in a footnote). Example: the forgetful functor U : Grp → Set is represented by (Z, ±1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalizer (universal fork)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f,g : X ⇒ Y, an equalizer is an object E and map e : E → X such that f ◦ e = g ◦ e and for every q : A → X with f ◦ q = g ◦ q there is a unique h : A → E with q = e ◦ h.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in Set: E = {x ∈ X | f(x) = g(x)} with inclusion into X; equalizers are unique up to unique isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel as equalizer
rubrics_metrics.description: In a category with a zero object, the kernel of f : A → B is defined as the equalizer of f and the zero map A → B; ker f : Ker f → A is a monomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation distinguishes the map ker f and the object Ker f; Proposition: equalizers are monic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cokernel as coequalizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Dually, the cokernel of f : A → B is the coequalizer of f and the zero map A → B; coker f : B ↠ Coker f is an epimorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of coker f as 'B modulo the image of f' (one must check normality issues in non-abelian examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image as kernel of cokernel
rubrics_metrics.description: The image Im f of f : A → B is defined as Ker(coker f); there is a canonical map im f : A → Im f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Im f exists it coincides with the concrete notion of image; universality gives a unique factorization A → Im f → B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additive category
rubrics_metrics.description: An additive category A is one with a zero object and (finite) products, and such that each Hom_A(A,B) is an abelian group with composition distributing over addition: (g + h) ◦ f = g ◦ f + h ◦ f and f ◦ (g + h) = f ◦ g + f ◦ h.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The zero map serves as the identity element; informally, 'in an additive category you can add two morphisms.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Abelian category
rubrics_metrics.description: An abelian category is an additive category in which every morphism has a kernel and cokernel, and every morphism factors through its image so that im(f) is epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vect_k, Ab, Mod_R are abelian; Grp is not even additive. In abelian categories many familiar exactness properties hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monic ⇔ trivial kernel
rubrics_metrics.description: In an abelian category, a map f is monic if and only if its kernel is the zero morphism 0 → A (i.e. Ker f ≅ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The easy direction holds even in some non-abelian contexts; the text gives an exercise/proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic ⇔ trivial cokernel
rubrics_metrics.description: Dually, a map f is epic if and only if its cokernel is the zero morphism B → 0 (i.e. Coker f ≅ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the dual statement to the monic/kernel criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism ⇔ monic and epic
rubrics_metrics.description: In an abelian category, a morphism is an isomorphism if and only if it is both monic and epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes the Mitchell embedding theorem justifies many such intuitions by reducing to module categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness at an object (categorical definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence ... → A_{n−1} −f_n→ A_n −f_{n+1}→ A_{n+1} → ... is exact at A_n if f_{n+1} ∘ f_n = 0 and the canonical map Im f_n → Ker f_{n+1} is an isomorphism; the sequence is exact if this holds at every object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short exact sequence 0 → A → B → C → 0 encodes C ≅ B/A along with the maps; exactness can be broken into short exact sequences using images and kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: First isomorphism theorem in abelian categories
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A → B in an abelian category there is an exact sequence 0 → Ker f → A → Im f → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the usual first isomorphism theorem (e.g. rank-nullity in Vect_k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freyd–Mitchell embedding theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a small abelian category then there exists a ring R and a full, faithful, exact functor from A into the category of left R-modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: to prove statements about abelian categories one may often reduce to the concrete case of modules and use 'diagram chasing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary operator on singular simplices
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a singular n-simplex σ with ordered vertices [v_0,...,v_n], define ∂(σ) := Σ_i (-1)^i [v_0,...,v_{i−1},v_{i+1},...,v_n]; extend linearly to n-chains. By convention a 0-chain has empty boundary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This orients faces with alternating signs; examples: ∂([v0,v1]) = [v1] − [v0], ∂([v0,v1,v2]) = [v0,v1] − [v0,v2] + [v1,v2].

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary squared equals zero (∂^2 = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any chain c, ∂(∂(c)) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is a sign-checking cancellation similar to previous parity sign exercises; this property is central to defining homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain groups, cycles, and boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: For a space X, C_n(X) is the free abelian group of singular n-chains; Z_n(X) := ker(∂ : C_n → C_{n−1}) are cycles and B_n(X) := im(∂ : C_{n+1} → C_n) are boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One checks B_n ⊆ Z_n ⊆ C_n and these are abelian groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology groups H_n
rubrics_metrics.description: The nth homology group is H_n(X) := Z_n(X) / B_n(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and consequences: H_0(X) ≅ Z^{#components}; H_1(X) for path-connected X is the abelianization of π_1(X) (Hurewicz theorem); examples computed for annulus, S^1, figure-eight, S^2, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurewicz theorem (for H_1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is path-connected then H_1(X) is the abelianization of π_1(X, x_0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: cycles correspond to loops, boundaries correspond to null-homotopic loops, and homology forces commutativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology splits over path components
rubrics_metrics.description: If X = ⨆_α X_α is a decomposition into path-connected components, then H_n(X) ≅ ⊕_α H_n(X_α); in particular, if there are r components then H_0(X) ≅ Z^r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute H_0 and reduce computations to components.
